## Overview

The Hatuqay are one of the twelve major Circassian tribes and are represented by one of the twelve stars on the green-and-gold Circassian flag. Their ancestral language is the Hatuqay dialect of Adyghe. Historically, they lived in the Hatuqay Principality of Circassia and were known for their martial character. Their original territory lay near the Black Sea coast, around the Taman peninsula and the southern banks of the Kuban, near the Afips River. In the late eighteenth century, the principality moved west of the Temirgoys, between the Belaya and Pshish rivers. Today, nearly all Hatuqays live in the diaspora. Most live in Turkey, including approximately 20 villages in Kayseri’s Pınarbaşı district, especially in the Çörümşek valley, as well as communities in Bozüyük, Bolu and Sakarya.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Evliya Çelebi’s account says that Hatuqay villages had mosques and that travelers stayed in private homes, while also stating that the villages had no churches, bazaars, markets, inns or bathhouses.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Evliya Çelebi describes Hatuqay soldiers as skilled with quivers, silver-inlaid gear and weapons.

## Music & performance

They do record a spoken and oral language culture. Evliya Çelebi described the Circassian language as a sound produced from the throat, cheeks and under the tongue, comparing it to a sparrow’s chirp and saying that he could not write it down. He also characterized the people as not literate in his account.

The sources describe oral and ceremonial forms connected with religion. Islam entered Circassian culture through stories and folk tales rather than directly. Ceremonies celebrating the birth of the Islamic prophet Muhammad played an important role, and a genre of Circassian epic literature associated with these celebrations emerged under the name *Mewlid*.

The Hatuqays were also associated with public speech and oratory. Aslandjeriy, one of the best-known Hatuqay princes, was noted for his character and oratorical skill.

## Festivals & rituals

They do, however, describe several customs and religious practices.

According to Evliya Çelebi, when a son was born while a guest was present in the house, the child was named after the guest. If there was no guest, the child was given the name of a neighbor. The account also says that a wet nurse took the boy to another place and raised him, feeding him better than his parents could.

The sources connect the celebration of the Islamic prophet Muhammad’s birth with the development of Mewlid, a genre of Circassian epic literature. They also state that mosques existed in Hatuqay villages and that people chanted “la ilahe illallah,” although the account says that they continued older traditions and did not fully grasp Islam. They do state that Aslandjeriy ordered every slave in the Hatuqay Principality to be freed according to Islamic obligations, after which slave families in the Hatuqay region were emancipated.

## Foodways

They do provide observations about food and religious practice in Evliya Çelebi’s account.

That account says that the people declared “La ilahe illallah” but ate fat pigs beginning from the tail. It also says that they did not fast or perform the daily prayers and that they did not permit anyone who did not own a pig to enter the village. The broader article identifies the Hatuqays as Sunni Muslims and states that they were among the first Circassian tribes to embrace Islam.

## Oral tradition & literature

Almost all knowledge about the founding of the Hatuqay Principality and tribe is described as coming from oral history. According to these accounts, the founding dynasty descended from King Inal. Prince Hatuqo was the grandson of Inal, the son of Chemrug and the brother of Prince Boletoqo, who was the first prince of the Chemguy Principality. After Inal’s death, the Chemguy Principality was divided, and Hatuqo moved west to establish a new principality.

A related legend says that Chemguy and Hatuqay were originally one people ruled by three brothers: Boletoqo, Zan and Hatuqo. The twins Boletoqo and Hatuqo slept beneath one fur cloth, which was found torn in two the next morning. Their mother cried, “Woe unto you, Chemirgoy! They have torn you asunder!” Later, Zan and Hatuqo separated from Boletoqo, and Hatuqo migrated west with his subjects.

The Hatuqay oral corpus also includes Nart sagas. The Adyghe Encyclopedia is said to compare Hattian mythology with Nart sagas, including stories found in the Hatuqay Nart corpus. The sources additionally record the folk etymology connecting Hatuqay with the Hittites, although the article distinguishes this from the proposed derivation of the name from Prince Hatuqo.

## Language & religion

The Hatuqays speak the Hatuqay dialect of Adyghe, a Western Circassian language. Hatuqay is classified among the “Steppe dialects,” together with Temirgoy, Abzakh and Bzhedug, while also sharing grammatical and phonological features with the “Coastal Dialects” of Shapsug and Natukhaj. It is described as an in-between dialect and as the closest Western dialect to Eastern Circassian. The sources associate this with frequent interaction with Kabardians in Kayseri, where Hatuqays are a minority among a Kabardian majority.

Today, a small community lives in Adygea, although its members speak the Temirgoy dialect. Hatuqays in Kfar Kama speak the Shapsug dialect.

The Hatuqays are Sunni Muslims. Islam entered Circassian culture through stories and folk tales, with ceremonies celebrating the birth of the Islamic prophet Muhammad contributing to the emergence of Mewlid literature. Evliya Çelebi’s account says that Hatuqay villages had mosques and that people chanted “la ilahe illallah,” while also maintaining older customs.
